title: Grandmaster Naroditsky | Ruy Lopez & Philidor | Chess History

moves.spoken: One last game against a 1600 who trots out the Scandinavian, meeting our king-pawn with an immediate central strike.
He recaptures with the queen, and this is the whole problem with the Scandi: the queen is out early and about to become a target.
teaches: Scandinavian: the early queen is exposed to tempo

moves.spoken: The knight to c3 is the best move — it develops a piece and gains a free tempo by hitting the queen.
teaches: Develop with tempo against the exposed queen

moves.spoken: He retreats all the way home to d8, so we've already gained ground for nothing.
We seize the full center with d4 — space and a big development lead, exactly the dream against a passive Scandinavian.
teaches: Occupy the center when ahead in development

moves.spoken: He just shuffles pawns with b5, doing nothing for his development. There's no special reply needed — we simply keep bringing pieces out.
teaches: Answer aimless pawn moves by continuing development

moves.spoken: So the bishop goes to d3, a simple, natural post aiming at his kingside.
We centralize the knight on e5, a powerful outpost right in the heart of his camp.
teaches: A knight on e5 is a dominant central outpost

moves.spoken: And the bishop develops to g5, pinning his knight. Nothing fancy yet — just getting every piece to a good square, fast, while he flounders.

Now the queen swings to f3 to pile on the pressure. I'm deliberately leaving the d4-pawn hanging: he's so underdeveloped that if the queen grabs it, she'll be hunted down and the lost tempo will cost him far more than a pawn.
teaches: A development lead is worth more than a pawn
plans: Offer d4 as bait — the greedy queen becomes a target
